newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rebound after big sell-off sparked by jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rebound after big sell-off sparked by jobs data.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks staged a recovery after tumbling in early trading Friday as long-term bond interest rates soared to the highest levels in three months amid fresh signs of economic strength.
The news, which came in the form of a surprisingly strong December employment report, sent the bond market into a tailspin that dragged stocks down.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 67 points in early trading, after the government reported that the economy added 262,000 jobs in December, far above Wall Street estimates of 192,000. The unemployment rate was unchanged at 5.3 percent.

By 1 p.m. EST, however, the 30-stock Dow index was 22.71 points higher at 6,648.38, surpassing its record closing high of 6,625.67 Thursday. The decline earlier led the New York Stock Exchange to activate its curbs on programme trading.
In the broader market, decliners outpaced advances by 14 to eight on volume of 305 million on the New York Stock Exchange.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell more than 1-1/2 points, boosting its yield to 6.88 percent from 6.75 percent on Thursday. The yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, was the highest since 6.92 percent on Sept. 30. Inflation is a bond investor's worst enemy as it erodes the returns on long-term investments.

Stocks were able to avoid the bond market's fate for a number of reasons, said analysts. One was that for stocks, the news was not all bad, because a strong economy bodes well for many companies' profits.
Perhaps more importantly, said analysts, investors showed themselves still committed to buying stocks on any dip.

"I think it's particularly the case in technology stocks where the view is, 'I want to buy them but not at these high prices,'" said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities. "When there's a dip, people step in and buy."
Technology stocks were in fact the first to rebound from the initial sell-off, pushing the Nasdaq Composite briefly into positive territory this morning.

"If this market turns around today, it's because Nasdaq turned it around," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "The market still wants to buy the big names on Nasdaq."
The Nasdaq 100 index, which includes the largest Nasdaq-listed companies, rose 5.75 points to 862.70.
The Nasdaq Composite index edged up 2.82 to 1,329.02.
Interest sensitive stocks were hit hard by the data, which included a surprising 262,000 increase in non-farm payrolls.
Economists had forecasted about 190,000 new jobs in December. Wages also beat expectations, rising 0.5 percent vs. forecasts for a 0.2 percent increase.
Bank stocks slid in sympathy with bonds. Citicorp fell 1-1/2 to 100-1/4, BankAmerica Corp. lost 1-1/8 to 97-1/4 and Wells Fargo & Co. shed 4-1/2 to 276-1/2.
The interest-rate-sensitive transportation sector was also broadly weaker. Delta Air Lines Inc. shed 1 to 71-1/4 and railroad giant Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corp. fell 2-1/8 to 86-1/8.
Cyclical, or economically sensitive, issues fared well, benefiting from the more robust economic outlook. Aluminum Co. of America rose 1-3/8 to 71 and General Motors Corp. rose 3/4 to 60.
Motorola Inc. was the NYSE's most active issue, rising 2-7/8 to 66-7/8 despite reporting lower-than-expected fourth quarter earnings last night.

Several Wall Street firms upgraded the shares on the belief that Motorola had turned the corner on its tough times. Motorola's recent woes have included a sharp correction in its semiconductor market and weak mobile telephone sales.
